claim: PIMT is abundantly expressed in mouse lung endothelium.
source: PIMT is abundantly expressed in mouse lung endothelium and PIMT deficiency in mice exacerbated pulmonary inflammation and vascular leakage to LPS(lipopolysaccharide).
evidence: The manuscript states this directly in the abstract and provides immunofluorescent staining data in Figure 1G showing PIMT localization to endothelium.

claim: PIMT deficiency in mice exacerbated pulmonary inflammation and vascular leakage to LPS.
source: PIMT is abundantly expressed in mouse lung endothelium and PIMT deficiency in mice exacerbated pulmonary inflammation and vascular leakage to LPS(lipopolysaccharide).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from Pimt+/− mice showing increased BALF protein, leukocytes, neutrophils, and cytokines compared to WT mice after LPS treatment (Figure 1A-C).

claim: PIMT inhibited LPS-induced toll-like receptor signaling through its interaction with TRAF6.
source: Furthermore, we found that PIMT inhibited LPS-induced toll-like receptor signaling through its interaction with TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) and its ability to methylate asparagine residues in the coiled-coil domain.
evidence: The manuscript provides co-immunoprecipitation data showing PIMT-TRAF6 interaction (Figure 3E) and luciferase assays showing PIMT inhibits TRAF6-induced NF-κB activation (Figure 3A).

claim: PIMT methylates asparagine residues in the coiled-coil domain of TRAF6.
source: Furthermore, we found that PIMT inhibited LPS-induced toll-like receptor signaling through its interaction with TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) and its ability to methylate asparagine residues in the coiled-coil domain.
evidence: The manuscript presents mass spectrometry data identifying methylation of N350 in the coiled-coil domain of TRAF6 (Figure 4D).

claim: PIMT interaction with TRAF6 inhibits TRAF6 oligomerization.
source: This interaction was found to inhibit TRAF6 oligomerization and autoubiquitination, which prevented NF-κB transactivation and subsequent expression of endothelial adhesion molecules.
evidence: The manuscript shows by co-immunoprecipitation that PIMT overexpression reduces TRAF6 oligomerization (Figure 4A).

claim: PIMT interaction with TRAF6 inhibits TRAF6 autoubiquitination.
source: This interaction was found to inhibit TRAF6 oligomerization and autoubiquitination, which prevented NF-κB transactivation and subsequent expression of endothelial adhesion molecules.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates by ubiquitination assay that PIMT overexpression reduces TRAF6 autoubiquitination (Figure 4B).

claim: PIMT prevents NF-κB transactivation.
source: This interaction was found to inhibit TRAF6 oligomerization and autoubiquitination, which prevented NF-κB transactivation and subsequent expression of endothelial adhesion molecules.
evidence: The manuscript shows by luciferase reporter assay that PIMT overexpression reduces NF-κB promoter activity (Figure 2A-B).

claim: PIMT suppressed ICAM-1 expression by inhibiting its N-glycosylation.
source: Separately, PIMT also suppressed ICAM-1 expression by inhibiting its N-glycosylation, causing effects on protein stability that ultimately translated into reduced EC(endothelial cell)-leukocyte interactions.
evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data showing PIMT overexpression causes a shift from high molecular weight to low molecular weight ICAM-1 (Figure 5A) and mass spectrometry data showing conversion of N-glycosylation sites to Asp (Figure 5G).

claim: PIMT inhibition of ICAM-1 N-glycosylation causes effects on protein stability.
source: Separately, PIMT also suppressed ICAM-1 expression by inhibiting its N-glycosylation, causing effects on protein stability that ultimately translated into reduced EC(endothelial cell)-leukocyte interactions.
evidence: The manuscript shows by cycloheximide chase assay that the low molecular weight form of ICAM-1 has increased degradation rate (Figure 6D).

claim: PIMT reduces EC-leukocyte interactions.
source: Separately, PIMT also suppressed ICAM-1 expression by inhibiting its N-glycosylation, causing effects on protein stability that ultimately translated into reduced EC(endothelial cell)-leukocyte interactions.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates by monocyte adhesion assay that PIMT overexpression reduces THP-1 cell adhesion to endothelial cells (Figure 6E).

source: The activation of the IKK complex causes phosphorylation of IκBα, which leads to polyubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation.

source: The liberated NF-κB dimer then translocates to the nucleus wherein it binds to specific DNA sequences to promote the expression of cytokines and endothelial adhesion molecules (Dunne and O'Neill, 2003; Szmitko et al., 2003).

claim: TRAF6 mediates immune responses through lysine 63 (K63)-linked ubiquitination of diverse signaling intermediators.
source: TRAF6 is a RING-domain cognate ubiquitin ligase (E3) associated with the intracellular domain of the IL-1R/TLR that mediates immune responses through lysine 63 (K63)-linked ubiquitination of diverse signaling intermediators (Chen, 2005; Deng et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chen, 2005; Deng et al., 2000).

source: As another hallmark of the vascular inflammatory process, leukocyte-endothelial adhesion is mediated by interactions between endothelial adhesion molecules and cognate receptors on immune cells (Szmitko et al., 2003).

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Springer, 1994; Staunton et al., 1988).

claim: Ligand-induced ICAM-1 cross-linking acts as a signal transducer to promote proinflammatory effects.
source: In addition, ligand-induced ICAM-1 cross-linking acts as a signal transducer to promote proinflammatory effects (Lawson and Wolf, 2009).

claim: N-glycosylation is indispensable for the proper conformation and biological function of ICAM-1 during inflammatory responses.
source: ICAM-1 is heavily N-linked glycosylated on extracellular Ig-like domains, and previous studies have demonstrated that this post-translational modification (PTM) is indispensable for the proper conformation and biological function of ICAM-1 during inflammatory responses (Chen et al., 2014b).

source: However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of ICAM-1 glycosylation remain largely unknown.

source: As a conserved protein repair enzyme, PIMT utilizes S-adenosyl methionine (SAM/AdoMet) to form methyl esters on carboxyl positions of isoaspartyl (isoAsp) residues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PIMT enzymatic function.

claim: IsoAsp is generated from asparagine (Asn) deamidation or aspartate (Asp) dehydration via succinimide intermediate under physiological or stressed conditions.
source: IsoAsp is generated from asparagine (Asn) deamidation or aspartate (Asp) dehydration via succinimide intermediate under physiological or stressed conditions and usually disrupts protein structure and/or function (Geiger and Clarke, 1987; Reissner and Aswad, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Geiger and Clarke, 1987; Reissner and Aswad, 2003).

claim: IsoAsp usually disrupts protein structure and/or function.
source: IsoAsp is generated from asparagine (Asn) deamidation or aspartate (Asp) dehydration via succinimide intermediate under physiological or stressed conditions and usually disrupts protein structure and/or function (Geiger and Clarke, 1987; Reissner and Aswad, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Geiger and Clarke, 1987; Reissner and Aswad, 2003).

claim: The methylated intermediate releases a methyl group to reform succinimide through spontaneous decomposition, which converts isoAsp to Asp in order to restore protein function.
source: The methylated intermediate then releases a methyl group to reform succinimide through spontaneous decomposition, which converts isoAsp to Asp in order to restore protein function (Desrosiers and Fanélus, 2011; Mishra and Mahawar, 2019; Reissner and Aswad, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Desrosiers and Fanélus, 2011; Mishra and Mahawar, 2019; Reissner and Aswad, 2003).

claim: Asn deamidation is significantly engaged in diverse biological functions such as cell apoptosis and the control of metabolic responses under inflammatory and stress conditions.
source: It is increasingly recognized that Asn deamidation is significantly engaged in diverse biological functions such as cell apoptosis and the control of metabolic responses under inflammatory and stress conditions (Deverman et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Deverman et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2020).

source: PIMT-mediated protein carboxyl methylation (O-methylation) was recently reported to be critically important for cells, indicating it may functionally rival other types of protein PTMs (Sprung et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Sprung et al., 2008).

source: For instance, overexpression of PIMT has been shown to extend longevity of bacteria, fruit flies, and plants (Chavous et al., 2001; Ogé et al., 2008; Pesingi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chavous et al., 2001; Ogé et al., 2008; Pesingi et al., 2017).

source: PIMT deficient mice exhibit increased isoAsp residual deposition and early neurological death due to grand mal seizures (Kim et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Kim et al., 1997).

source: Furthermore, we and others have shown that PIMT plays an important role in angiogenesis and cardiomyocyte survival under oxidative conditions (Ouanouki and Desrosiers, 2016; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Ouanouki and Desrosiers, 2016; Yan et al., 2013).

claim: PIMT acts by inhibiting LPS-induced NF-κB activation through methylation of TRAF6 in ECs.
source: Mechanistically, we show that PIMT acts by inhibiting LPS-induced NF-κB activation through methylation of TRAF6 in ECs and by physically interacting with ICAM-1 to impact N-glycosylation and its functional interactions with immune cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents mass spectrometry data showing TRAF6 methylation (Figure 4D) and functional assays showing inhibition of NF-κB activation (Figure 2A-B).

claim: PIMT physically interacts with ICAM-1 to impact N-glycosylation.
source: Mechanistically, we show that PIMT acts by inhibiting LPS-induced NF-κB activation through methylation of TRAF6 in ECs and by physically interacting with ICAM-1 to impact N-glycosylation and its functional interactions with immune cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents co-immunoprecipitation data showing PIMT-ICAM-1 interaction (Figure 5D-E) and mass spectrometry data showing altered N-glycosylation sites (Figure 5G).

claim: PIMT-mediated protein O-methylation plays a central role in controlling vascular inflammation in the lung.
source: In summary, our findings suggest that PIMT-mediated protein O-methylation plays a central role in controlling vascular inflammation in the lung.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing PIMT effects on inflammation and vascular function.

claim: Susceptibility to ALI was significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice following LPS injury.
source: Following LPS injury, we found that susceptibility to ALI was significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased BALF protein, leukocytes, neutrophils, cytokines, and lung injury in Pimt+/− mice compared to WT mice after LPS treatment (Figure 1A-F).

claim: Total protein levels in BALF were significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice compared to WT counterparts after LPS injury.
source: This correlated with increased total protein levels and numbers of total leukocytes and neutrophils in isolated bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from Pimt+/− mice compared to WT counterparts (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Figure 1A shows quantitative data of BALF protein concentrations in WT and Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment.

claim: Numbers of total leukocytes in BALF were significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice compared to WT counterparts after LPS injury.
source: This correlated with increased total protein levels and numbers of total leukocytes and neutrophils in isolated bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from Pimt+/− mice compared to WT counterparts (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Figure 1A shows quantitative data of BALF cell counts in WT and Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment.

claim: Numbers of neutrophils in BALF were significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice compared to WT counterparts after LPS injury.
source: This correlated with increased total protein levels and numbers of total leukocytes and neutrophils in isolated bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) from Pimt+/− mice compared to WT counterparts (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows quantitative data of BALF neutrophil counts in WT and Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment.

claim: BALF cytokine and chemokine levels for TNF-α, IL-6 and Ccl2 were significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice after LPS injury.
source: Furthermore, we found that BALF cytokine and chemokine levels for TNF alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6) and C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (Ccl2) were also significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Figure 1C shows ELISA data of TNF-α, IL-6, and Ccl2 levels in BALF from WT and Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment.

claim: Baseline expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and Ccl2 was indistinguishable between Pimt+/− and WT mice.
source: Baseline expression of TNF-α, interleukin 1 beta (IL-1β), IL-6, and Ccl2 was indistinguishable between Pimt+/− and WT mice.
evidence: Figure 1D shows qRT-PCR data indicating no significant difference in baseline mRNA levels of these cytokines between genotypes.

claim: After LPS instillation, mRNA levels for TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and Ccl2 were significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice compared to WT controls.
source: However, after LPS instillation, mRNA levels for these factors were significantly increased in Pimt+/−- mice compared to WT controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating significantly higher mRNA levels of these cytokines in Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment.

claim: Expression of adhesion molecule ICAM-1 was significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment, as determined by qRT-PCR.
source: Likewise, the expression of adhesion molecule ICAM-1 was also significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice, as determined by both quantitative real-time RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) (Figure 1D) and western blot (Figure 1E).
evidence: Figure 1D shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating significantly higher ICAM-1 mRNA levels in Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment.

claim: Expression of adhesion molecule ICAM-1 was significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment, as determined by western blot.
source: Likewise, the expression of adhesion molecule ICAM-1 was also significantly increased in Pimt+/− mice, as determined by both quantitative real-time RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) (Figure 1D) and western blot (Figure 1E).
evidence: Figure 1E shows western blot data demonstrating significantly higher ICAM-1 protein levels in Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment.

claim: Histological analysis displayed exaggerated lung injury in PIMT+/− mice, as manifested by the presence of increased alveolar hemorrhage, infiltration of inflammatory cells into distal air sacs and disruption of alveolar walls in response to LPS.
source: Histological analysis displayed exaggerated lung injury in PIMT+/− mice, as manifested by the presence of increased alveolar hemorrhage, infiltration of inflammatory cells into distal air sacs and disruption of alveolar walls in response to LPS (Figure 1F).
evidence: Figure 1F shows H&E staining of lung sections and quantification of infiltrated immune cells in WT and Pimt+/− mice after LPS treatment.

claim: Immunofluorescent staining localized PIMT expression to the endothelium.
source: Immunofluorescent (IF) staining localized PIMT expression to the endothelium (Figure 1G), suggesting endothelial PIMT expression may be important for regulating lung inflammation.
evidence: Figure 1G shows immunofluorescent staining of PIMT co-localized with CD31 (endothelial marker) in mouse lung sections.

claim: Endothelial PIMT expression may be important for regulating lung inflammation.
source: Immunofluorescent (IF) staining localized PIMT expression to the endothelium (Figure 1G), suggesting endothelial PIMT expression may be important for regulating lung inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization of PIMT to endothelium and the observed effects of PIMT deficiency on lung inflammation.

claim: LPS has been known to stimulate the expression of inflammatory molecules in ECs via the TLR-NF-κB pathway.
source: LPS has been known to stimulate the expression of inflammatory molecules in ECs via the TLR-NF-κB pathway (Dauphinee and Karsan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Dauphinee and Karsan, 2006).

claim: Overexpression of PIMT markedly reduced the NF-κB driven luciferase activity under both basal and LPS-stimulated conditions.
source: EA.hy926 endothelial cells were transiently transfected with a plasmid containing a heterologous promoter driven by NF-κB elements upstream of the luciferase gene (Ahn et al., 1995), and overexpression of PIMT markedly reduced the NF-κB driven luciferase activity under both basal and LPS-stimulated conditions.
evidence: Figure 2A shows luciferase assay data demonstrating reduced NF-κB activity with PIMT overexpression.

claim: Ectopic expression of an inactive PIMT mutant (PIMT-Del) had limited effect on LPS-induced NF-κB activation.
source: By contrast, ectopic expression of an inactive PIMT mutant, which has a deleted catalytic motif I (PIMT-Del; Kagan and Clarke, 1994), had limited effect on LPS-induced NF-κB activation (Figure 2A and B), suggesting the enzymatic activity is indispensable for inhibitory function.
evidence: Figure 2A shows luciferase assay data demonstrating that PIMT-Del does not significantly reduce NF-κB activity.

claim: The enzymatic activity of PIMT is indispensable for its inhibitory function on NF-κB activation.
source: By contrast, ectopic expression of an inactive PIMT mutant, which has a deleted catalytic motif I (PIMT-Del; Kagan and Clarke, 1994), had limited effect on LPS-induced NF-κB activation (Figure 2A and B), suggesting the enzymatic activity is indispensable for inhibitory function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the inactive PIMT mutant does not inhibit NF-κB activation.

claim: Knockdown of PIMT expression by lentivirus expressing PIMT shRNAs significantly augmented LPS-stimulated NF-κB promoter-driven luciferase activity.
source: Meanwhile, knockdown of PIMT expression by lentivirus expressing PIMT shRNAs(small hairpin RNAs) significantly augmented LPS-stimulated NF-κB promoter-driven luciferase activity, as compared with the control shRNA (sh-Ctrl; Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows luciferase assay data demonstrating increased NF-κB activity with PIMT knockdown.

claim: PIMT depletion augmented the expression of adhesion molecules and cytokines, including ICAM-1, VCAM1, TNF-α, IL-6, and Ccl2, in HUVECs under both basal and LPS-stimulated conditions.
source: In human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), PIMT depletion also augmented the expression of adhesion molecules and cytokines, including ICAM-1, vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM1), TNF-α, IL-6, and Ccl2, as determined by qPCR, under both basal and LPS-stimulated conditions (Figure 2D), while adenovirus-mediated PIMT overexpression suppressed the expression of inflammatory molecules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2D shows qRT-PCR data demonstrating increased mRNA levels of these molecules with PIMT knockdown.

claim: Adenovirus-mediated PIMT overexpression suppressed the expression of inflammatory molecules in HUVECs.
source: In human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), PIMT depletion also augmented the expression of adhesion molecules and cytokines, including ICAM-1, vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM1), TNF-α, IL-6, and Ccl2, as determined by qPCR, under both basal and LPS-stimulated conditions (Figure 2D), while adenovirus-mediated PIMT overexpression suppressed the expression of inflammatory molecules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows qPCR data demonstrating decreased mRNA levels of inflammatory molecules with PIMT overexpression.

claim: PIMT is a novel negative regulator of NF-κB activation in ECs.
source: Collectively, these results suggest PIMT is a novel negative regulator of NF-κB activation in ECs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing PIMT inhibits NF-κB activation and inflammatory molecule expression.

claim: IKKβ and IκBα phosphorylation levels were significantly attenuated by PIMT overexpression at different time points after LPS stimulation.
source: Consistent with this, we found that IKKβ and IκBα phosphorylation levels were significantly attenuated by PIMT overexpression at different time points after LPS stimulation compared with control adenovirus (Ad-LacZ; Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2E shows western blot data demonstrating reduced phosphorylation of IKKβ and IκBα with PIMT overexpression after LPS treatment.

claim: LPS-induced IKKβ and IκBα phosphorylation were further augmented in PIMT depleted cells.
source: Furthermore, LPS-induced IKKβ and IκBα phosphorylation were further augmented in PIMT depleted cells as compared with the sh-Ctrl transduced cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Figure 2F shows western blot data demonstrating increased phosphorylation of IKKβ and IκBα with PIMT knockdown after LPS treatment.

claim: LPS-induced nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit of NF-κB was significantly reduced in PIMT overexpressing cells.
source: Moreover, LPS-induced nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit of NF-κB, as determined by western blot and IF staining, was significantly reduced in PIMT overexpressing cells (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Figure 2G shows western blot data and Figure 2H shows immunofluorescent staining demonstrating reduced nuclear p65 with PIMT overexpression after LPS treatment.

claim: NF-κB DNA binding capacity was significantly inhibited by overexpressing PIMT in ECs.
source: NF-κB DNA binding capacity, as detected by electrophoretic mobility-shift assay (EMSA), was significantly inhibited by overexpressing PIMT in ECs (Figure 2I).
evidence: Figure 2I shows EMSA data demonstrating reduced NF-κB DNA binding with PIMT overexpression after LPS treatment.

claim: PIMT inhibits LPS-induced endothelial NF-κB activation through acting on IKKβ kinase or its upstream regulators.
source: Together, these results indicate that PIMT inhibits LPS-induced endothelial NF-κB activation through acting on IKKβ kinase or its upstream regulators.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing PIMT affects IKKβ and IκBα phosphorylation.

claim: TRAFs are critically involved in TNF receptors and TLR/IL-1 signaling pathways that lead to NF-κB activation.
source: TRAFs are critically involved in TNF receptors and TLR/IL-1 signaling pathways that lead to NF-κB activation (Chen, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Chen, 2005).

claim: Overexpression of PIMT in ECs significantly inhibited the NF-κB activation induced by TRAF2 and TRAF6, but not by IKKβ-SS/EE.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, overexpression of PIMT in ECs significantly inhibited the NF-κB activation induced by TRAF2 and TRAF6, but not by IKKβ-SS/EE, a constitutively active mutant of IKKβ (Nottingham et al., 2014).
evidence: Figure 3A shows luciferase assay data demonstrating PIMT inhibits TRAF2- and TRAF6-induced NF-κB activation but not IKKβ-SS/EE-induced activation.

claim: PIMT was substantially enriched in the anti-TRAF6 immunocomplex, as compared with anti-TRAF2 or anti-IKKβ immunocomplexes.
source: Our co-IP demonstrated that PIMT was substantially enriched in the anti-TRAF6 immunocomplex, as compared with anti-TRAF2 or anti-IKKβ immunocomplexes (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows co-immunoprecipitation data demonstrating stronger interaction between PIMT and TRAF6 compared to TRAF2 or IKKβ.

claim: The interaction of PIMT with TRAF6 was confirmed by forward and reciprocal co-IP assays.
source: The interaction of PIMT with TRAF6 was further confirmed by forward and reciprocal co-IP assays (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Figure 3C and D show co-immunoprecipitation data confirming PIMT-TRAF6 interaction in both directions.

claim: The endogenous interaction of TRAF6 with PIMT was confirmed by co-IP in both HUVECs and HLMVECs.
source: The endogenous interaction of TRAF6 with PIMT was confirmed by co-IP using an anti-PIMT antibody in both HUVECs and human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVECs; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B show co-immunoprecipitation data demonstrating endogenous PIMT-TRAF6 interaction in endothelial cells.

claim: The endogenous interaction of PIMT with TRAF6 was augmented by LPS stimulation.
source: Noteworthy, this endogenous interaction was augmented by LPS stimulation.
evidence: Figure 3E shows co-immunoprecipitation data demonstrating increased PIMT-TRAF6 interaction after LPS treatment.

claim: PIMT expression was marginally influenced by LPS in vivo or in cultured HLMVECs.
source: Given the fact that PIMT expression was marginally influenced by LPS in vivo or in cultured HLMVECs (Figure 1E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), these data strongly indicate that dynamic interaction of PIMT and TRAF6 may constitute an important negative feedback mechanism in resolving LPS inflammation.
evidence: Figure 1E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C show western blot data demonstrating minimal change in PIMT expression after LPS treatment.

claim: Dynamic interaction of PIMT and TRAF6 may constitute an important negative feedback mechanism in resolving LPS inflammation.
source: Given the fact that PIMT expression was marginally influenced by LPS in vivo or in cultured HLMVECs (Figure 1E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), these data strongly indicate that dynamic interaction of PIMT and TRAF6 may constitute an important negative feedback mechanism in resolving LPS inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PIMT-TRAF6 interaction increases with LPS stimulation while PIMT expression remains constant.

claim: TRAF6 consists of a RING domain at its N-terminus, followed by zinc finger (ZnF) domains, a coiled-coil (CC) domain, and a TRAF-C domain at the C-terminus.
source: TRAF6 is an ubiquitin E3 ligase which consists of a RING domain at its N-terminus, followed by zinc finger (ZnF) domains, a coiled-coil (CC) domain, and a TRAF-C domain at the C-terminus (Chung et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Chung et al., 2002).

claim: HA-tagged TRAF6 lacking the N-terminal RING domain and ZnF domains was efficiently pulled down by Flag-tagged PIMT.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, HA-tagged TRAF6 lacking the N-terminal RING dom ain and ZnF domains was efficiently pulled down by Flag-tagged PIMT, while further deletion of the CC domain comprehensively abolished the interaction.

claim: Deletion of the CC domain of TRAF6 comprehensively abolished the interaction with PIMT.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, HA-tagged TRAF6 lacking the N-terminal RING dom ain and ZnF domains was efficiently pulled down by Flag-tagged PIMT, while further deletion of the CC domain comprehensively abolished the interaction.

claim: The CC domain of TRAF6 is responsible for the binding of PIMT in TRAF6.

claim: Enzymatic activity of PIMT is required for the inhibition of TRAF6 function.
source: Similarly, the polyubiquitination of TRAF6 was exclusively inhibited by PIMT-WT (Figure 4B), suggesting that enzymatic activity of PIMT is required for the inhibition of TRAF6 function.

claim: TAK1 activation has been implicated in LPS-mediated TLR signaling.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Irie et al., 2000).

claim: D339 and N350, located in the CC domain of TRAF6, were methylated in PIMT expressing cells.

claim: Both PIMT-modified and unmodified N350 are present in PIMT depleted cells.
source: As expected, ~50% knockdown of PIMT would not completely abolish all of these methylations. Both PIMT-modified and unmodified N350 are present in PIMT depleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).

claim: N350 deamination was abundantly detected in both PIMT expressing and knockdown cells.
source: Interestingly, in addition to methylation, N350 deamination was abundantly detected in both PIMT expressing and knockdown cells, suggesting that the N350 deamination is naturally present regardless of the level of PIMT in cells.
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1D shows mass spectrometry data detecting N350 deamination in PIMT expressing cells.

claim: N350 deamination is naturally present regardless of the level of PIMT in cells.
source: Interestingly, in addition to methylation, N350 deamination was abundantly detected in both PIMT expressing and knockdown cells, suggesting that the N350 deamination is naturally present regardless of the level of PIMT in cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that N350 deamination is detected in both PIMT expressing and knockdown cells.

claim: N350 is followed by a glycine, which is a typical 'hot spot' for deamidation and subsequent O-methylation by PIMT.
source: Since N350 is followed by a glycine, which is a typical 'hot spot' for deamidation and subsequent O-methylation by PIMT (Reissner and Aswad, 2003), we speculated that deamination of N350 can be further methylated in PIMT expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Reissner and Aswad, 2003) and represents established knowledge about PIMT substrate specificity.

claim: Deamination of N350 can be further methylated in PIMT expressing cells.
source: Since N350 is followed by a glycine, which is a typical 'hot spot' for deamidation and subsequent O-methylation by PIMT (Reissner and Aswad, 2003), we speculated that deamination of N350 can be further methylated in PIMT expressing cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known substrate specificity of PIMT and the detection of N350 methylation.

claim: D339 and N350 sites are conserved among species.
source: D339 and N350 sites are conserved among species (Figure 4E).
evidence: Figure 4E shows sequence alignment demonstrating conservation of D339 and N350 across species.

claim: Overexpression of D339A and N350A mutants in EA.hy926 cells significantly activated NF-κB to the similar extent as WT TRAF6.

evidence: Figure 4F shows luciferase assay data demonstrating that D339A and N350A mutants activate NF-κB similarly to WT TRAF6.

claim: Co-overexpression of PIMT markedly inhibited both WT TRAF6- and D339A mutant-induced NF-κB transactivation but minimally affected N350A-induced NF-κB transactivation.
source: Importantly, co-overexpression of PIMT markedly inhibited both WT TRAF6- and D339A mutant-induced NF-κB transactivation but minimally affected N350A-induced NF-κB transactivation, suggesting that N350 O-methylation is involved in the PIMT-mediated suppression of NF-κB activation.
evidence: Figure 4F shows luciferase assay data demonstrating differential effects of PIMT on WT, D339A, and N350A TRAF6-induced NF-κB activation.

claim: N350 O-methylation is involved in the PIMT-mediated suppression of NF-κB activation.
source: Importantly, co-overexpression of PIMT markedly inhibited both WT TRAF6- and D339A mutant-induced NF-κB transactivation but minimally affected N350A-induced NF-κB transactivation, suggesting that N350 O-methylation is involved in the PIMT-mediated suppression of NF-κB activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the N350A mutant is resistant to PIMT-mediated inhibition.

claim: N350A mutation specifically attenuated PIMT-mediated inhibition of TRAF6 oligomerization and autoubiquitination.
source: Furthermore, N350A mutation also specifically attenuated PIMT-mediated inhibition of TRAF6 oligomerization and autoubiquitination (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Figure 4G and H show co-immunoprecipitation and ubiquitination assay data demonstrating that N350A mutation reduces PIMT's ability to inhibit TRAF6 oligomerization and autoubiquitination.

claim: O-methylation of TRAF6 at N350 is critically involved in the regulation of TRAF6 function and subsequent NF-κB activation by PIMT.
source: Together, these findings suggest that O-methylation of TRAF6 at N350 is critically involved in the regulation of TRAF6 function and subsequent NF-κB activation by PIMT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing N350 is methylated by PIMT and N350A mutation prevents PIMT-mediated inhibition of TRAF6.

source: Here, we found that overexpression of PIMT not only attenuated TNF-α-stimulated expression of ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 in a dose-dependent manner but also induced a surprise shift of protein bands high molecular weight (HMW) to lower molecular weight (LMW) forms (Figure 5A), which we speculate represents a partially glycosylated form of protein.

claim: The LMW form of ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 represents a partially glycosylated form of protein.

claim: Similar results of PIMT effects on ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 were observed in LPS- and IL-1β-treated HUVECs and HLMVECs.

claim: PIMT does not significantly impact the global glycosylation pattern in ECs.

No significant disparity was observed in Ad-LacZ- and Ad-PIMT-transduced ECs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows PHA-L staining data demonstrating no significant difference in global glycosylation between control and PIMT-overexpressing cells.

claim: PIMT knockdown efficiently increased ICAM-1 protein levels in ECs.
source: Additionally, we found PIMT knockdown by lentiviral shRNAs efficiently increased ICAM-1 protein levels in ECs, as determined by western blot (Figure 5C) and flow cytometry (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and the adhesion of monocytes to activated ECs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C show western blot and flow cytometry data demonstrating increased ICAM-1 levels with PIMT knockdown.

claim: PIMT knockdown increased the adhesion of monocytes to activated ECs.

evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1D shows monocyte adhesion assay data demonstrating increased THP-1 cell adhesion to endothelial cells with PIMT knockdown.

claim: ICAM-1 is essentially involved in both adhesion and extravasation of leukocytes during inflammation.
source: Since ICAM-1 is essentially involved in both adhesion and extravasation of leukocytes during inflammation, it was chosen to further define the molecular mechanism of how ICAM-1 glycosylation was regulated by PIMT1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ICAM-1 function.

claim: PIMT interacts only with LMW ICAM-1 (~70 kDa) but not with HMW ICAM-1 (~110 kDa).
source: We used moderate multiplicity of infection (moi = 5) of Ad-PIMT to induce both HMW and LMW ICAM-1 and then performed co-IP. Our results showed that PIMT interacts only with LMW ICAM-1 (~70 kDa) but not with HMW ICAM-1 (~110 kDa; Figure 5D and E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), suggesting this interaction impairs the processing of ICAM-1 glycosylation in ECs.
evidence: Figure 5D, E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E show co-immunoprecipitation data demonstrating selective interaction between PIMT and LMW ICAM-1.

claim: PIMT interaction with LMW ICAM-1 impairs the processing of ICAM-1 glycosylation in ECs.
source: We used moderate multiplicity of infection (moi = 5) of Ad-PIMT to induce both HMW and LMW ICAM-1 and then performed co-IP. Our results showed that PIMT interacts only with LMW ICAM-1 (~70 kDa) but not with HMW ICAM-1 (~110 kDa; Figure 5D and E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), suggesting this interaction impairs the processing of ICAM-1 glycosylation in ECs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PIMT selectively interacts with the LMW (less glycosylated) form of ICAM-1.

claim: ICAM-1 possesses a C-terminal cytoplasmic domain, a single transmembrane domain, and an extracellular domain containing eight N-glycosylation sites.

source: Eight Asn residuals have been described as N-glyco sites in ICAM-1 in previous studies (Casasnovas et al., 1998; Shimaoka et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2004), while in PIMT overexpression samples, four of them were identified to be switched to Asp residues, which are incapable of linking N-glycans (Figure 5G; Figure S3C-E).

claim: Asp residues are incapable of linking N-glycans.
source: Eight Asn residuals have been described as N-glyco sites in ICAM-1 in previous studies (Casasnovas et al., 1998; Shimaoka et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2004), while in PIMT overexpression samples, four of them were identified to be switched to Asp residues, which are incapable of linking N-glycans (Figure 5G; Figure S3C-E).

claim: All four Asn sites converted to Asp by PIMT were positioned in the antigen-binding regions of ICAM-1 extracellular Ig domains.

evidence: Figure 5H shows a schematic diagram indicating the positions of the deamidated residues in ICAM-1 structure.

claim: Both HMW and LMW forms of ICAM-1 were localized to the cell surface.

claim: Glycosylation deficient ICAM-1 is able to escape the surveillance of endoplasmic reticulum quality control (ERQC) and localize to the cell membrane.
source: Furthermore, cell surface biotinylation assay revealed that both HMW and LMW forms of ICAM-1 were localized to the cell surface (Figure 6B), suggesting that glycosylation deficient ICAM-1 is able to escape the surveillance of endoplasmic reticulum quality control (ERQC) and localize to the cell membrane (Jørgensen et al., 2003).

claim: Pre-treatment with tunicamycin significantly attenuated ICAM-1 crosslinking aroused signaling.
